question: Can a class-balanced, isotonic-calibrated LightGBM model give more reliable win/loss judgements than a standard random forest on game states, as a small stand-in for checking a player's reading of game rules?
method: Stratified 75/25 split (seed 42) of OpenML tic-tac-toe endgame data; one-hot encoded cells; baseline 300-tree random forest vs. class-balanced LightGBM with 5-fold CV grid search and isotonic calibration; seeds 42-44; accuracy main, F1/Brier/log loss secondary.
baseline: Standard RandomForestClassifier (300 trees) on one-hot cells, raw probabilities.
improved: LightGBM with class_weight='balanced', hyper-parameters chosen by 5-fold CV grid search on the training set (neg. log loss), wrapped in isotonic calibration (5-fold internal CV on training data).
notes: Stand-in experiment, not a replication of the paper's logic-based method. Only one stratified split was used (seed 42) per the split-once rule; seeds 42-44 vary the models only, so the std reflects model randomness, not split variability. The test set (about 240 rows) is small, so accuracy differences of a few points are within noise. Grid search and calibration use only training data. fetch_openml takes no timeout argument, so a socket-level 60 s timeout is set globally. Compute is matched only roughly: the improved model runs a small grid search plus calibration.
